subject_title: Reliability, Resilience, Chaos, and Recovery Assurance
theoretical_foundations:
Reliability is a conditional probability, not an intrinsic percentage: R(t | u,e,c) = P(T > t | use profile u, environment e, configuration c), where T is time to an unacceptable service failure. Requirements therefore state the mission, exposure, environment, failure definition, and observation window. The dependability vocabulary separates a fault (a hypothesized cause, such as a latent defect, broken link, bad input, or operator action), an error (an erroneous internal state that can propagate), and a failure (a deviation of delivered service from the specified behavior). The usual causal chain is fault -> error -> failure; detection, containment, masking, recovery, or correction can break the chain. Faults may be latent or active, transient, intermittent, or permanent, and may arise from design, physical, interaction, or operational causes. These distinctions prevent a process crash, a stale replica, a corrupted record, and a user-visible outage from being counted as the same event. Reliability is failure-free operation for a specified interval and profile; availability is the probability of being in an acceptable service state at a time (including explicitly defined degraded states); maintainability describes the distribution of repair or restoration time; resilience is the dynamic ability to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to adversity while maintaining required capability. Resilience has no universally accepted scalar, so a capability trajectory is useful: plot delivered capability q(t) before, during, and after disruption, record minimum acceptable capability, degradation duration, recovery time, and whether adaptation leaves the system in a safe and correct state.

Core mathematics should be used with assumptions visible. For lifetime distribution F(t), reliability R(t)=1-F(t), density f(t), and hazard h(t)=f(t)/R(t). MTTF is integral from 0 to infinity of R(t) dt for a non-repairable item. For a two-state repairable model with failure rate lambda and repair rate mu, steady-state availability is A=mu/(lambda+mu)=MTTF/(MTTF+MTTR) when rates are stationary and exponential; a transient continuous-time Markov chain instead solves p'(t)=p(t)Q, and multi-state availability is the sum of probabilities of all states whose service is acceptable. Reliability block diagrams give R_series=product(R_i) and R_parallel=1-product(1-R_i) only under the stated independence and common mission assumptions. Replicas in the same zone, image, control plane, provider, or operator process have correlated/common-cause failures, so the parallel formula overstates assurance; quorum and beta-factor or explicit common-cause models are preferable for high-criticality designs. In a continuous-time Markov model, solve pi Q=0, sum(pi)=1, and sum pi_i over acceptable states; state-space growth and non-exponential behavior are important limits.

Reliability growth is a learning process, not proof that a defect population has been exhausted. The empirical Duane form uses cumulative failure rate C(t)=N(t)/t=a t^(-alpha), or log C(t)=log a-alpha log t; a positive alpha indicates declining cumulative failure rate under a stable test-and-fix process. The Crow/AMSAA nonhomogeneous Poisson process represents mean cumulative failures M(t)=lambda t^beta and intensity m(t)=lambda beta t^(beta-1); beta<1 indicates improvement, beta=1 a constant rate, and beta>1 deterioration. Software-specific Goel-Okumoto models use M(t)=a(1-exp(-bt)) and intensity ab exp(-bt), while the Musa-Okumoto logarithmic model uses a decreasing intensity of the form lambda_0/(1+theta lambda_0 t). Fit parameters with maximum likelihood or an explicitly documented alternative, show confidence or credible intervals, test goodness of fit and residuals, and report the operational-profile time used. Models assume an identified failure process, representative exposure, known or consistently classified failures, and a correction process whose effect is meaningful. Architecture changes, changing workloads, imperfect debugging, duplicate reporting, censoring, and fixes that introduce new defects invalidate naive extrapolation. A model forecast should be a decision input with uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, never a release guarantee.

Resilience is engineered through layered fault tolerance and containment. Error detection may be concurrent (checksums, invariants, heartbeats, sequence checks) or preemptive (health probes, leases, admission checks); containment limits propagation to a failure domain; recovery returns the component or service to a correct state; fault handling removes or isolates the cause. Useful boundaries are process, service, queue, tenant, cell, zone, region, and provider boundaries. Mechanisms include bulkheads, bounded queues, backpressure, deadlines, bounded retry budgets with jitter, circuit breakers, idempotency keys, deduplication, load shedding, safe read-only or stale-data modes, transactional outboxes, fencing tokens, quorum, and explicit split-brain prevention. Redundancy may be active-active, active-passive, N+1, or m-of-n; diversity (different implementations, versions, regions, providers, or operational paths) can reduce common-mode risk but adds testing, deployment, reconciliation, and operator complexity. Graceful degradation must preserve stated invariants rather than silently dropping correctness or safety.

Recovery assurance treats restoration as a correctness property, not merely process liveness. RTO is the maximum allowed unavailability before unacceptable impact; RPO is the latest recoverable point in time and therefore the measured data-loss bound; MTD is the maximum tolerable disruption and normally exceeds RTO because validation, backlog processing, and business resumption consume time. Specify recovery targets per business capability and dependency, then measure observed values from a precisely defined disruption trigger to validated service. A restore is successful only after cryptographic or content checks, schema/version compatibility checks, row or object counts where meaningful, referential and domain invariants, ordering and idempotent replay checks, duplicate-side-effect checks, authorization of normal workflows, and an explicit return-to-normal or handback test. Backups should have independent failure domains, retention and version metadata, immutable or offline copies where risk warrants, regular restore sampling, and documented evidence that the tested artifact is the artifact the plan names. Failover requires fencing or leases, a quorum or equivalent authority, write-order and replay semantics, dependency readiness, and a deliberate handback; otherwise active-active designs can create split brain or stale writes.

Chaos engineering and fault injection are controlled experiments about system behavior under a specified fault model. A defensible experiment has a pre-registered steady-state hypothesis (for example, “under loss of one zone, valid requests remain above the agreed threshold, no acknowledged writes are lost, and recovery reaches the target within the measured RTO”), a baseline period, a treatment fault, a control or comparison where feasible, explicit abort thresholds, an independent kill switch, and a post-experiment restoration and invariant check. Start with reversible process or dependency faults in an isolated environment; then expand by risk assessment to a single production failure domain with narrow time, tenant, region, and intensity bounds. The injector should be declarative and auditable, with target identity, fault type, intensity, start/stop time, owner, authorization, abort conditions, rollback action, and immutable configuration hash. Preflight verifies target, backup/restore readiness, dependency health, and rollback reachability. Faults should be selected from incident and defect data as well as theoretical coverage: process termination, node or zone loss, dependency error, network loss/delay/partition, message duplication or reordering, stale discovery, clock skew, read-only or unavailable storage, quota exhaustion, and backup/restore failure. Avoid irreversible data corruption until a separately approved, isolated test can prove cleanup. Initial experiments vary one material fault at a time; later designs can test correlated failures, but must identify confounders. Record timestamps, target state, fault actions, steady-state measurements, human decisions, aborts, recovery steps, and semantic validation. A passing experiment establishes evidence for the tested fault, topology, workload, and time window only; it does not prove all-fault reliability.

An enterprise 2026 SDLC should make this evidence cumulative. During requirements, maintain a service criticality and failure-mode register, define acceptable and degraded modes, RTO/RPO/MTD, data-loss semantics, and measurable invariants. During architecture, perform FMEA/FTA/RBD or Markov analysis for high-consequence paths, document independence and common-cause assumptions, and select containment and recovery boundaries. During implementation, test recovery handlers, idempotency, fencing, replay, and safe degradation as first-class code; require dependency contracts to state recovery behavior. In CI and pre-production, run deterministic fault-injection suites and restore tests; in operations, schedule risk-based game days and controlled production experiments with automatic aborts. Release evidence should include reliability-growth data with model uncertainty, observed RTO/RPO distributions and confidence bounds, restore correctness results, unresolved common causes, and assumptions that were not exercised. For multi-region, edge, event-driven, and agentic services, include vendor/control-plane loss, nondeterministic or unavailable model dependencies, replay-safe side effects, deterministic/manual fallback, and cross-team handback. A mature evidence packet links the requirement, fault model, experiment configuration, raw measurements, recovery artifacts, semantic checks, decision, and follow-up regression test.

Evidence limits and disagreements must remain explicit. Chaos practice has strong engineering rationale but limited independent causal evidence that experiments alone improve organizational reliability; published success cases are selected and often lack randomized controls. Fault injections can be too artificial, too low-level, or too clean compared with gray failures, correlated supplier failures, human action, and data corruption. Reliability-growth curves can fit historical failures while extrapolating poorly across changing architecture, operational profile, or correction policy. Availability nines hide denominator choices, maintenance exclusions, degraded states, and user-level correctness. MTBF is not a next-failure probability for nonstationary software, and MTTR can be gamed by excluding detection, validation, or planned work. Redundancy improves independent-failure probability but may amplify correlated failure, reconciliation, and operational complexity. A game day demonstrates the exercised roles, artifacts, and scenario, not a rare catastrophe that was not represented. RTO/RPO and ISO/NIST-aligned plans are normative or managerial objectives; only repeatable, scenario-specific tests establish achieved capability. No named model or standard is universally effective: select it by failure semantics, consequence, data quality, independence assumptions, and the cost and safety of experimentation.
practical_architecture_and_implementatio:
Architecture and implementation should use a closed assurance loop: (1) define service and data invariants, criticality, failure domains, degraded modes, RTO/RPO/MTD, and ownership; (2) enumerate fault sources and propagation paths with FMEA, fault trees, reliability blocks, dependency graphs, or CTMCs as appropriate; (3) choose containment, redundancy, diversity, detection, and recovery mechanisms; (4) encode recovery and degradation behavior as testable code and runbooks; (5) exercise faults and restores under controlled hypotheses; (6) validate semantics and handback; and (7) feed measured failures and near misses into design, models, and regression tests.

A minimal experiment specification should contain: experiment ID and revision; service, version, tenant/cell/zone/region, and dependency targets; fault class and intensity; start/stop schedule; steady-state indicators and threshold; expected capability under degradation; control/comparison definition; preflight checks; authorization and owner; automatic abort thresholds; independent kill switch; rollback/cleanup; backup and restore readiness; data-safety restrictions; and evidence retention. Injectors should be capability-limited, time-bounded, idempotent, and auditable. Begin with staging or a disposable replica, then a single failure domain. Production execution requires a low-risk target, a tested abort path, no unresolved dependency outage, a recovery owner on duty, and explicit limits on data mutation. Do not use chaos as a substitute for security penetration testing or nominal capacity testing.

Fault-containment patterns include bounded timeouts and retry budgets, jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads and per-tenant queues, backpressure, load shedding, idempotency keys, deduplication, transactional outbox/inbox processing, leases and fencing, quorum writes, safe read-only or cached modes, and explicit dependency fallbacks. Every retry must have a deadline and a termination condition. Every fallback must state freshness and correctness bounds. Every active-active writer must have conflict resolution and a split-brain prevention mechanism. Every active-passive failover must prove promotion authority, stale-primary fencing, dependency readiness, and handback. Replicas should cross independent zones and, where justified, regions, providers, software versions, or operating teams; document residual common-cause risk instead of treating placement as independence.

Backup and recovery implementation should maintain a catalog of artifacts, ownership, retention, encryption/integrity metadata, schema and code versions, dependency assumptions, and restore instructions. At least one copy should be in an independently failing domain; immutable or offline copies are proportionate controls for destructive scenarios. Restore tests should use the actual production-format artifact into an isolated environment, record start/end times, and check checksums, object/row counts, schema compatibility, referential and domain invariants, ordering, duplicate side effects, replay/idempotency, and representative end-to-end transactions. A full failover test should time detection, decision, promotion, dependency reconfiguration, service recovery, semantic validation, backlog drain, and handback separately. Report RTO/RPO as distributions or bounded observations by scenario, not as a single best-case number.

Evidence should be reproducible: preserve the hypothesis, baseline window, raw measurements, injector and system configuration hashes, timestamps, abort events, operator actions, restored artifact identity, validation outputs, and model version. Compare runs across representative operational profiles; distinguish injected-fault outcomes from unrelated incidents and planned maintenance. For reliability growth, retain failure classification, execution exposure, correction action, fix verification, and censoring decisions; fit multiple plausible models when data allow and show parameter uncertainty. For recovery, maintain an evidence matrix mapping each business capability to tests, dates, scenario, achieved RTO/RPO, semantic checks, open assumptions, and next exercise.

A risk-based cadence is preferable to a universal schedule. Run unit and component recovery tests on every material code path change, integration failover and restore tests on dependency or schema changes, tabletop and game-day exercises at a cadence set by consequence and change rate, and full cross-domain recovery tests before claiming a new RTO/RPO tier. Review after incidents, near misses, architecture changes, provider changes, and unexplained model residuals. A 2026 enterprise may add policy-as-code guardrails, automated experiment admission, multi-region and agentic-service fallbacks, and evidence graphs, but automation must not remove human authority for high-consequence aborts or handback decisions.

primary_evidence.source_title: Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Algirdas Avižienis, Jean-Claude Laprie, Brian Randell, Carl E. Landwehr
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: a generic concept including as special case such attributes as reliability, availability, safety, integrity, maintainability, etc.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This foundational IEEE taxonomy supplies the vocabulary needed to separate reliability, availability, maintainability, faults, errors, failures, fault tolerance, recovery, and forecasting. In the 2026 SDLC, requirements and test evidence should name the attribute and failure semantics being demonstrated; an uptime result cannot stand in for data integrity or correct recovery.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: George Candea, Aaron B. Brown, Armando Fox, David Patterson
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Building systems to recover fast may be more productive than aiming for systems that never fail.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The recovery-oriented argument supports investing in short, correct recovery paths, micro-restart or scoped restart, state safeguarding, and measured MTTR rather than relying only on preventive perfection. It does not eliminate prevention: fast recovery must preserve state, avoid repeated failure, and be validated for correctness.

primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: the most-used operations will have received the most testing
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: Operational-profile testing makes reliability estimates conditional on how the service is actually used. Enterprise teams should weight reliability-growth and fault-injection scenarios by mission exposure and separately test rare but high-consequence operations; otherwise a low failure rate can reflect an unrepresentative workload rather than robust software.

primary_evidence.source_title: Learning Curve Approach to Reliability Monitoring
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: On a Log-Log Plot, the graph of Cumulative Failure Rate Vs Cumulative Test Time is Linear.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The Duane postulate motivates log-log reliability-growth plots and a simple learning-curve diagnostic. In current software, use it to inspect whether test-analyse-fix data exhibit a stable trend, but report fit uncertainty and profile or architecture changes; the empirical line is not a universal law or a release threshold.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Many large tech organizations are using experimentation to verify the reliability of such systems.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The peer-reviewed chaos-engineering framing supports hypothesis-driven reliability experiments in distributed systems. Its descriptive claim is not proof that every organization benefits equally; enterprise adoption should add explicit steady-state metrics, blast-radius limits, aborts, comparison data, and semantic recovery checks.

primary_evidence.source_title: Assessing Dependability with Software Fault Injection: A Survey
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Roberto Natella, Domenico Cotroneo, Henrique S. Madeira
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: Software Fault Injection is a method to anticipate worst-case scenarios caused by faulty software
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The ACM survey places software fault injection inside dependability assessment and emphasizes selecting techniques for representativeness, efficiency, and usability. For a 2026 test program, fault models should be traceable to incidents, defect classes, and architecture boundaries, not only to easy-to-inject process kills; injection outcomes are scenario evidence, not field-failure probabilities.

primary_evidence.source_title: Efficient Testing of Recovery Code Using Fault Injection
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: A critical part of developing a reliable software system is testing its recovery code.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This ACM study directly supports treating recovery handlers as test targets despite their low nominal execution frequency. Apply library- or boundary-level injection to exercise error returns and environmental faults, then assert state safety, idempotency, and completion—not merely that a handler ran.

primary_evidence.source_title: SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Marianne Swanson, Pauline Bowen, Amy Phillips, Dean Gallup, David Lynes)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: RTO defines the maximum amount of time that a system resource can remain unavailable before there is an unacceptable impact
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NIST gives RTO a mission-impact meaning rather than treating it as a generic engineering aspiration. Pair it with RPO (recoverable point and tolerated data loss) and MTD, assign values per business capability, and verify each with timed failover or restore evidence that includes validation and resumption work.

primary_evidence.source_title: SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Tim Grance, Tamara Nolan, Kristin Burke, Rich Dudley, Gregory White, Travis Good)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: A test is an evaluation tool that uses quantifiable metrics to validate the operability of a system or system component
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NIST distinguishes quantifiable system tests from training and discussion-based exercises. A recovery program should combine component tests, timed failover and restore tests, tabletop/game-day decisions, and after-action improvement; a conversation alone cannot establish achieved RTO/RPO.

primary_evidence.source_title: SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Ron Ross, Victoria Pillitteri, Richard Graubart, Deborah Bodeau, Rosalie McQuaid)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: the capability to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to adverse conditions
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: NIST’s resilience framing is broader than uptime and explicitly includes adaptation. It supports requirements for normal, degraded, and recovered capability, with resilience experiments that test transitions and mission outcomes; the document is security-oriented, so this module applies its general resilience concepts without importing penetration methods.

primary_evidence.source_title: SP 1339, OT Backup Quick Start Guide
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: creating them regularly, testing them, and reviewing them during recovery exercises.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: This current NIST guidance makes backup assurance an operational lifecycle: create, test, and review during exercises. For enterprise services, retain artifact identity and semantic restore evidence; a successful backup job without a tested restore is not recovery assurance.

primary_evidence.source_title: ISO 22301:2019, Security and resilience — Business continuity management systems — Requirements
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: plan for a return to normal business
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: ISO’s continuity framing includes the transition back from the alternate or degraded state. Recovery plans and game days should therefore test handback, backlog reconciliation, data consistency, and operational ownership—not stop when a standby endpoint answers. Certification or plan conformity is governance evidence, not a substitute for scenario-specific technical tests.

primary_evidence.source_title: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software engineering — Product quality model
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: The characteristics and subcharacteristics provide a reference model for the quality of the products to be specified, measured and evaluated.
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The product-quality model supports turning reliability and recoverability into specified and measured quality properties rather than informal slogans. Use it as a reference model and tailor characteristics, measures, and thresholds to the system; it does not prescribe one universal availability or recovery target.

primary_evidence.source_title: Probability and Its Applications to Reliability, Quality Control, and Risk Assessment (MIT OpenCourseWare 22.38)
primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Nuclear Science and Engineering (Michael Golay)
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: methods for reliability and risk assessment of complex systems (event-tree and fault-tree analysis, common-cause failures, human reliability models)
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: MIT courseware anchors the quantitative toolkit and highlights common-cause and human reliability as necessary complements to component independence assumptions. An enterprise model should select fault trees, event trees, Markov models, Monte Carlo, or Bayesian methods by system structure and data, then expose uncertainty and human-action assumptions.

primary_evidence.authors_or_institution: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission; W. E. Vesely, F. F. Goldberg, N. H. Roberts, D. F. Haasl
primary_evidence.verbatim_excerpt: this handbook has been developed as text for the System Safety and Reliability Course
primary_evidence.analytical_interpretation: The NRC handbook provides a formal, inspectable way to decompose top events into combinations of basic failures. Use fault trees to challenge hidden single points and common causes, but supplement them with dynamic state, repair, human, and data-corruption analysis where static Boolean assumptions are insufficient.

failure_modes_and_antipatterns: Availability-only success: the endpoint is reachable but acknowledged writes, ordering, referential integrity, or user-visible business invariants are lost. Require semantic validation after failover and restore.

RTO/RPO theater: objectives are printed in a plan but detection, decision, validation, backlog drain, and handback are omitted from the clock. Measure observed distributions from a defined disruption trigger.

Hidden common cause: replicas share a zone, provider, image, deployment controller, DNS, identity service, schema, clock, operator, or backup catalog. Model dependencies and correlated failure explicitly.

Retry amplification: timeouts and unbounded retries convert a dependency fault into queue growth, duplicate side effects, or a cascading outage. Bound retries, deadlines, queue size, and concurrency; test the limits.
Split-brain failover: two writers promote without fencing or quorum, producing stale reads, conflicting writes, or unreconcilable state. Test promotion authority, fencing, replay, and handback.

Untested backups: jobs report success, but artifacts are incomplete, incompatible with current schemas, corrupted, inaccessible, or never restored. Test actual production-format artifacts and preserve restore evidence.

Recovery-code neglect: recovery handlers have low code coverage because nominal tests rarely execute them, so first use during an incident is the first integration test. Inject boundary faults and assert correct state transitions.

Unrepresentative fault model: only process kills or clean latency faults are tested while gray failures, stale discovery, partial partitions, message duplication, storage errors, human action, and supplier/control-plane failures remain untested.

Oversized blast radius: an experiment lacks target validation, time bounds, independent abort, or a tested rollback and affects unrelated tenants or failure domains. Start isolated and expand only with explicit risk controls.

No baseline or confounded experiment: normal variation, concurrent deploys, incidents, or maintenance are mistaken for treatment effects. Record a baseline, comparison where feasible, environmental confounders, and exact injector configuration.

Game-day choreography: participants follow a familiar script or pre-alerted path that bypasses real decision latency, missing ownership, and handback uncertainty. Vary scenarios and include unscripted injects while retaining safe aborts.

Reliability-growth extrapolation error: a Duane, Crow/AMSAA, Goel-Okumoto, or Musa-Okumoto fit is extrapolated across architecture, workload, fix policy, or failure-class changes. Compare models, show uncertainty, and treat forecasts as conditional evidence.

MTBF misuse: a mean for a repairable or nonstationary process is presented as the probability of the next failure, or planned maintenance and detection delays are excluded from MTTR. State the stochastic model and denominator.
Replica diversity illusion: nominally different replicas depend on the same libraries, build pipeline, configuration, provider, or operator runbook. Test and document residual common-mode risk.
Gray-failure blindness: health checks pass while responses are stale, selectively wrong, slow, or semantically invalid. Define correctness and freshness invariants, not only process liveness.

Degraded-mode drift: graceful degradation silently removes a mission-critical function, violates safety or data guarantees, or persists after the dependency recovers. Specify degraded capability and automatic or governed restoration.

Recovery starts too early: services accept traffic before replicas, schemas, caches, queues, or downstream dependencies are consistent. Gate readiness on semantic checks and staged backlog reconciliation.

Human and organizational omission: role ambiguity, unavailable approvers, supplier coordination, or fatigue dominates recovery time but is absent from technical tests. Include decision rights, call paths, and cross-team handback in exercises.

False universalism: adopting a named standard, chaos method, target number of nines, or maturity label as proof of reliability. Applicability depends on consequence, data, independence, system dynamics, and evidence quality.

Security-scope leakage: using reliability experiments to perform unauthorized security or penetration actions, or injecting destructive faults without data-safety controls. Keep the experiment authorized, reversible, and within the reliability/recovery boundary.

maturity_matrix.foundational: Define fault, error, failure, reliability, availability, maintainability, resilience, degraded mode, RTO, RPO, and MTD for each critical capability. Maintain a dependency and failure-mode register; identify single points and common causes with simple FMEA, fault trees, or block diagrams. Establish basic R(t), availability, MTTF/MTTR assumptions, and a small reliability-growth dataset. Test recovery handlers, failover paths, backups, and restores in isolated environments; validate checksums, schemas, and core business invariants. Run tabletop exercises and timed restore tests with named owners, documented aborts, and evidence packets. Treat all targets as hypotheses until measured.
maturity_matrix.advanced: Use representative operational profiles and classified failure data for reliability-growth analysis with confidence intervals and model checks. Apply CTMC, RBD, fault-tree, event-tree, or simulation analysis to high-consequence paths, including common-cause and human assumptions. Implement layered containment, bounded retries, bulkheads, idempotency, fencing, quorum, safe degraded modes, cross-domain redundancy, and tested handback. Run scheduled component/integration fault injection, dependency failover, restore drills, and risk-based game days; use steady-state hypotheses, comparison data where feasible, independent kill switches, narrow blast radius, and semantic recovery gates. Track achieved RTO/RPO distributions per scenario and link findings to regression tests, architecture decisions, and dependency contracts.
maturity_matrix.expert_2026: Operate an evidence graph linking requirements, invariants, architecture boundaries, fault models, experiments, incidents, restores, model versions, and corrective actions. Select or ensemble reliability models based on data quality, nonstationarity, profile changes, and consequence; show uncertainty, residuals, sensitivity, and common-cause exposure. Automate policy-as-code admission and abort controls while reserving human authority for high-consequence decisions. Exercise multi-region, edge, provider/control-plane, supply-chain, event-driven, and agentic-service failures, including replay-safe side effects, nondeterministic dependency loss, deterministic/manual fallback, and handback correctness. Use independent challenge reviews, cross-organization game days, cryptographically or content-attested restore artifacts, adaptive fault-model coverage from incidents and near misses, and explicit evidence limits; never treat a standard, model, or chaos program as universal proof.
